item.title: Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe shows that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.
item.dc:creator: Jakub Zaj\k{a}c, Micha{\l} Dyrek

item.title: Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios
item.description: arXiv:2611.27274v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.
item.dc:creator: Paul Ruelloux, Christian Bongiorno, Damien Challet

item.title: Forecasting Realized Volatility with Time Series Foundation Models: A Comparison with Econometric Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2607.05291v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on large collections of series and forecast a new series without being trained on it. We compare nine TSFMs, used in this zero-shot setting, with eight econometric models, including the Heterogeneous Autoregressive (HAR) family. We forecast the realized volatility of 50 assets in equities, currencies and futures from the VOLARE dataset one, five and 22 days ahead, and compare the forecasts with pairwise and multi-model tests. The foundation models do not outperform the econometric benchmarks as a class. Only Tiny Time Mixers (TTM), the smallest of them, has a lower average QLIKE loss than the logarithmic HAR (Log-HAR) at every tested horizon, by a narrow margin. For most assets, the Model Confidence Set (MCS) contains TTM together with Log-HAR and several other models. Accuracy differs far more across the foundation models than between the best of them and Log-HAR, so which foundation model one chooses matters more than whether one uses a foundation model or an econometric one. For an investor who targets a constant volatility, TTM's edge is worth a few basis points a year before trading costs. Since TTM and Log-HAR make different errors, their equal-weight average matches the best single model and enters the MCS for nearly every asset.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Brini

item.title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
item.description: arXiv:2611.14325v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Brini
